recentItems.title: US and Denmark reach deal over Greenland | BBC News
recentItems.description:
The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize the territory by force.
 
The announcement comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns.
 
Trump said the agreement would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory.
 
The leaders of Denmark and Greenland welcomed the deal to "strengthen security" in the region.

Murdered women in South Africa spark Johannesburg protests | BBC News
recentItems.description:
Nine bodies of murdered women have been found in Johannesburg in similar circumstances since July.
 
Most of the victims were young, in their 20s or 30s, and almost all had suffered extreme violence before their deaths.
 
Women in the city have taken to the streets to march against the violence, after previous protests in South Africa over the high rates of femicide.

US v China - who’s ahead in the race to develop AI? | BBC Americast
recentItems.description:
We speak to a US/China tech expert who served under presidents Biden and Trump about America’s race with China to develop Artificial Intelligence. Does he agree with president Trump’s statement “whoever wins AI wins”, and what does “winning” look like?

Justin, Marianna and Anthony discuss Donald Trump’s rejection of any regulation for Artificial Intelligence, and whether this is in line with public opinion in the United States.

The team also talk about Congress, and how Republicans are reacting to Donald Trump’s most outspoken comments yet on AI. Plus, could Democrats be making the issue more central to their campaigning ahead of this November’s midterm elections? It’s an issue which has also united progressive Democrat senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon - what was their message to voters?

Our guest this week is Chris McGuire, a US-China technology expert with the Council on Foreign Relations. He’s a former senior advisor at the State Department for Trump in both his first and second terms, and previously served as Deputy Senior Director for Technology and National Security at the National Security Council from 2022 to 2024 under president Biden.

recentItems.title: Chaos as police move migrants to a camp in Ceuta | Global News Podcast
recentItems.description:
Police in Spain's North African territory of Ceuta used batons and fired rubber bullets into the air to control crowds, as they moved hundreds of migrants from beaches to a tent camp. Tens of thousands of migrants crossed from neighbouring Morocco to Ceuta in July. At least 100 people died in the attempt. Though most of the migrants went back, several thousand have remained in the Spanish territory.

recentItems.title: Houthis claim biggest advancement this year in Yemen | BBC News
recentItems.description:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels have made significant gains in Yemen on the Red Sea coast, impacting Saudi Arabian exports and contributing to the continued price of a barrel of oil at above $100.
 
Elsewhere, Saudi Arabia intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of the Islamic holy city of Mecca on Tuesday evening, according to the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen. The 57-nation Organisation of Islamic Cooperation said attacks on Mecca and Medina province, where Islam's second holiest shrine is located, constituted an "unacceptable and intolerable transgression".
 
Meanwhile, the US has allowed Iranian officials to attend the UN General Assembly next week in New York. The delegation will take part in the United Nations General Assembly's grand debate for 2026, but will face strict travel restrictions whilst they are in the country.

Trump bans CNN and Politico from White House | BBC News
recentItems.description:
President Trump has announced that he is "immediately" banning CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House, the latest twist in his fraught relationship with the media.

In a post on Truth Social on Friday, Trump said that the outlets "constantly write or report fiction or lies" about his administration, although he provided no examples.

Trump later called it a "very simple ban", but did not explain how it would work. It is unclear whether employees of those outlets would be prevented from entering the White House grounds.

CNN swiftly slammed the move as an "illegal assault" on American media freedoms. The move by Trump is likely to be met with legal challenges.

In a statement, the network called a potential ban illegal and said it "stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting."

"We have a right under the US Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government," the CNN statement said. "Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right."

In his post Trump said: "Media outlets shouldn't be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration or the United States of America. Other news outlets to follow."
The post did not mention specific stories or reporting that led to the move.

Asked about the ban in the Oval Office, Trump said:  "It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years," he said. "You get sick of it."

Jane Hill presents BBC News at Ten reporting by Sarah Smith in Washington.
